item.passage:
Most animals that live through northern winters avoid freezing in one of two ways: they migrate, or they shelter somewhere the temperature stays above the freezing point of their body fluids. The wood frog of North America, whose range reaches north of the Arctic Circle in Alaska and Canada, does neither. It spends the winter beneath a shallow layer of leaf litter, and when the temperature falls far enough, it freezes.

The freezing is not uniform. Ice forms in the spaces outside the cells, in the body cavity, and beneath the skin, while the fluid inside the cells stays liquid. In this state, which can last for weeks, the frog's heart stops beating and it does not breathe. Survival depends on what happens when ice first begins to form on the skin. Within minutes, the liver starts converting its stored glycogen into large amounts of glucose, which the blood carries to the organs before circulation stops. The sugar acts as a cryoprotectant: by raising the concentration of dissolved substances inside the cells, it limits how much water is drawn out of them as the surrounding fluid turns to ice, so that the cells do not shrink to a fatal degree.

There are limits to this tolerance. Laboratory studies suggest that frogs generally survive when up to roughly two-thirds of their body water has frozen, but not much more. In spring the ice melts, the heart begins beating again, and the frog soon moves on to breed in temporary ponds.

item.passage:
In lakes fed by melting glaciers, the mud on the bottom often builds up in thin, paired layers. Each spring and summer, meltwater streams carry sand and silt into the lake, and these relatively coarse particles settle quickly, forming a light-colored band. In winter, when the streams freeze and the lake's surface is covered by ice, the water becomes still, and the finest clay particles, which had remained suspended, slowly sink to form a thinner, darker band. One light band and one dark band together make up a varve, a deposit representing a single year.

Because each varve records one year, counting varves works much like counting tree rings. In the late nineteenth century, the Swedish geologist Gerard De Geer began measuring varves exposed in Swedish clay deposits. He noticed that the thickness of successive varves rose and fell in recognizable sequences, reflecting warm years with heavy melting and cold years with little. By matching these sequences from one site to the next, he linked overlapping records into a single chronology. Extended by later researchers, it covers roughly the last 13,000 years, the period during which the great ice sheet retreated across Sweden.

The method requires care. A sudden flood or an underwater landslide can deposit a layer that resembles an annual band, and a year with very little sediment may leave a layer too thin to see. Researchers therefore check varve counts against independent methods, such as radiocarbon dating of plant remains preserved in the layers.

item.passage:
Until the second half of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Clocks were set by the sun, so that noon was the moment the sun stood highest over that particular place. Because the Earth turns through one degree of longitude about every four minutes, a town some distance east of its neighbor would be several minutes ahead of it. For people who rarely traveled far, these differences hardly mattered.

The railways changed that. A train passing through many towns could not follow all of their clocks at once, and timetables printed in local time were confusing and, where trains shared a single track, dangerous. Railway companies responded by adopting standards of their own. In Britain, most lines had adopted London time by the late 1840s. In the United States, where distances were far greater, individual railroads used dozens of different standards, and a large station might display several clocks, each showing the time kept by a different company.

On November 18, 1883, the major railroads of the United States and Canada replaced these with a small number of time zones, each an hour apart, so that all clocks within a zone agreed. Many cities adopted railroad time quickly, although some resisted what they saw as interference with the natural time set by the sun. Standard time was the railroads' own arrangement, however; it did not become federal law in the United States until 1918.

item.passage:
Until the second half of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Clocks were set by the sun, so that noon was the moment the sun stood highest over that particular place. Because the Earth turns through one degree of longitude about every four minutes, a town some distance east of its neighbor would be several minutes ahead of it. For people who rarely traveled far, these differences hardly mattered.

The railways changed that. A train passing through many towns could not follow all of their clocks at once, and timetables printed in local time were confusing and, where trains shared a single track, dangerous. Railway companies responded by adopting standards of their own. In Britain, most lines had adopted London time by the late 1840s. In the United States, where distances were far greater, individual railroads used dozens of different standards, and a large station might display several clocks, each showing the time kept by a different company.

On November 18, 1883, the major railroads of the United States and Canada replaced these with a small number of time zones, each an hour apart, so that all clocks within a zone agreed. Many cities adopted railroad time quickly, although some resisted what they saw as interference with the natural time set by the sun. Standard time was the railroads' own arrangement, however; it did not become federal law in the United States until 1918.

item.passage:
In a well-known experiment published in 1999, the psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked participants to watch a short video of two teams passing basketballs and to count the passes made by the players wearing white. Partway through, a person in a gorilla costume walked into the middle of the scene, paused, and walked off. Roughly half of the viewers, absorbed in counting, did not notice the gorilla at all, and many were astonished when the video was replayed.

The phenomenon, which the researchers Arien Mack and Irvin Rock had named inattentional blindness, shows that seeing is not simply a matter of having an object in front of one's eyes. Attention acts as a filter. When it is fully occupied by a demanding task, objects outside that task can pass through the field of view without being consciously registered, even when they are large, unusual, and in plain sight. Importantly, the effect depends on what the observer is attending to. In related studies, unexpected objects that resembled the items being tracked were noticed more often than objects that differed from them.

The finding has practical implications. A driver talking on a phone, for instance, may look directly at a hazard and still fail to respond to it. At the same time, people tend to be confident that they would notice anything important that happened in front of them, a belief the experiment suggests is often mistaken.

item.passage:
In 1959, a very large natural gas field was discovered near Groningen in the northern Netherlands. Over the following years, gas exports brought substantial income into the country. Yet by the 1970s, observers noticed that Dutch manufacturing was struggling, and in 1977 the magazine The Economist gave the pattern a name: the Dutch disease. The term now describes a broader puzzle, in which a boom in one natural-resource sector appears to weaken other parts of an economy.

Economists usually explain the effect through prices. When foreign buyers pay for a country's resource exports, they must acquire its currency, and this added demand tends to push up the currency's value. A stronger currency makes the country's other exports, such as manufactured goods, more expensive abroad, while making imported goods cheaper at home. Domestic manufacturers are squeezed from both sides. At the same time, the booming sector may draw workers and investment away from other industries by offering higher wages.

The difficulty becomes clearest when the boom ends. Resources may run out or their world price may fall, and the industries that shrank during the boom cannot always be rebuilt quickly, because skills and businesses that were lost take years to replace. For this reason, some resource-rich governments have tried to limit the effect by saving part of their resource income abroad, often in large state funds, rather than spending all of it at home, which eases the pressure on the currency.

item.passage:
In true fresco, or buon fresco, the painter applies pigments mixed only with water to a layer of wet lime plaster. As the plaster dries, the lime reacts with carbon dioxide in the air and forms a crystalline layer of calcium carbonate that locks the pigment particles into the surface of the wall. Because the color becomes part of the plaster rather than resting on top of it, a well-made fresco can survive for centuries.

The technique imposes strict demands. Since the paint binds only while the plaster is damp, the artist could plaster only as much wall as could be painted in a single session, an area Italian painters called a giornata, or "day's work." The joins between these patches are often still visible to conservators, allowing them to estimate how many days a mural took. Mistakes were difficult to correct; the usual remedy was to cut away the plaster and begin that section again. In addition, some pigments, including certain blues, did not work well in wet lime and had to be added later, on the dry surface, in a method known as secco.

Painting on dry plaster gave artists more time and a wider range of colors, but the paint never bonded with the wall in the same way. Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper in Milan on a dry wall rather than in true fresco, and the painting began to deteriorate within a few decades. It has required repeated restoration ever since.

item.passage:
In true fresco, or buon fresco, the painter applies pigments mixed only with water to a layer of wet lime plaster. As the plaster dries, the lime reacts with carbon dioxide in the air and forms a crystalline layer of calcium carbonate that locks the pigment particles into the surface of the wall. Because the color becomes part of the plaster rather than resting on top of it, a well-made fresco can survive for centuries.

The technique imposes strict demands. Since the paint binds only while the plaster is damp, the artist could plaster only as much wall as could be painted in a single session, an area Italian painters called a giornata, or "day's work." The joins between these patches are often still visible to conservators, allowing them to estimate how many days a mural took. Mistakes were difficult to correct; the usual remedy was to cut away the plaster and begin that section again. In addition, some pigments, including certain blues, did not work well in wet lime and had to be added later, on the dry surface, in a method known as secco.

Painting on dry plaster gave artists more time and a wider range of colors, but the paint never bonded with the wall in the same way. Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper in Milan on a dry wall rather than in true fresco, and the painting began to deteriorate within a few decades. It has required repeated restoration ever since.
